findings.body: The docstring promises constant time and states records arrive in chronological order, yet the function sorts the whole list — O(n log n) work plus a full copy of the input — only to read the last element. findings.body: `label in seen` scans a list that grows by one entry per distinct label, so deduplicating n rows costs O(n^2) in the worst case. A `set` gives O(1) membership checks; the body would use `seen: set[str] = set()` and `seen.add(label)` instead of `seen.append(label)`.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows contains many distinct labels (e.g. a large payment export), each membership test rescans all previously seen labels, so runtime grows quadratically and the function stalls on large inputs.
findings.title: Use a set for the seen-label membership check

findings.body: The query has no LIMIT and `fetchall()` materialises every matching row, then copies each into a dict. If an owner can accumulate a large order history and no caller-side bound exists, memory and latency grow with table size; add pagination or a LIMIT to cap each fetch.

findings.title: Bound the order-row fetch with a limit or pagination

findings.body: The inner loops over zones and weights never reference `carrier`, so every carrier recomputes the identical count: total work is O(carriers x zones x weights). findings.body: The inner two loops never reference `carrier`, so every pass of the outer loop recomputes the exact same `count` — O(carriers × zones × weights) work and three levels of nesting to produce a single number. findings.body: owner_id is interpolated directly into the SQL text via an f-string, so any quote or SQL syntax in the value changes the meaning of the query (CWE-89). Make `seen` a `set[str]` (`seen: set[str] = set()` on the declaration line and `seen.add(label)` where it is appended) while keeping `labels` as the ordered output list; membership checks then become O(1) and the whole pass O(n). The restructure spans the whole function body, so no single-line replacement is shown.

findings.body: The query text is built one line above by f-string interpolation of owner_id directly into the SQL, so any caller-influenced value can break out of the quoted string and alter the statement. Bind the value through the driver's parameter mechanism instead of formatting it into the query, and delete the now-unused `query = f"..."` assignment. Placeholder syntax is driver-dependent (`%s` for psycopg2/MySQLdb, `?` for sqlite3).
findings.failure_scenario: If owner_id comes from request input, a value like ' OR '1'='1 turns the WHERE clause into a tautology and returns every customer's orders; a UNION or stacked payload can read or modify unrelated tables.

findings.title: SQL injection: bind owner_id as a query parameter
